title: Lagrangian field theory
one_line_summary: Builds the Lagrangian machinery for classical fields (action, Lagrangian density, Euler-Lagrange equations, tested on a vibrating string and the Klein-Gordon field), carries it into curved spacetime with sqrt(-g) and semicolons, varies the Einstein-Hilbert action to recover Einstein's equation, defines the energy-momentum tensor as the metric derivative of the matter Lagrangian, derives Noether currents from Killing symmetries, and finally extracts the relativistic Euler equation and the perfect-fluid T from a fluid Lagrangian.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part VI. Part II (ch12, ch13) obtained T and the field equation by physical guesswork; this chapter replaces that guesswork with a systematic variational recipe, using the Part V toolkit (volume form of ch37, covariant derivative of ch34, Lie derivative and Killing vectors of ch33, the log-determinant exercise of ch34). It follows ch39 on fluids, whose Euler equation and perfect-fluid tensor it re-derives, and it is the launch pad for the field-theory chapters that follow: scalar-field inflation (ch41), the electromagnetic field (ch42), gauge fields (ch44), gravitational waves obeying a wave equation (ch46) and quantum gravity/string theory (ch49). It is a spiral revisit of Einstein's equation, now as an equation of motion from an action.

assumed_background.topic: Action, Lagrangian and Euler-Lagrange equations for particles; relativistic free-particle action
Kinetic and potential energy of a stretched string; Hamiltonian mechanics and canonical momentum
Integration by parts, divergence theorem, differentials of multivariable functions
Matrix inverse, determinant, trace, matrix logarithm
Covariant derivative, connection coefficients and semicolon notation; metric compatibility
Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar
Einstein tensor and the field equation G = 8 pi T
Energy-momentum tensor, its conservation, and the perfect-fluid form
Lie derivative along a vector field and Killing vectors
Identity d ln det M = Tr(M^-1 dM) and divergence via sqrt(-g)
Faraday tensor F and Maxwell's theory
First law for adiabatic processes, internal energy and pressure
Idea that particles are quanta of fields (optional context)

learning_objectives: Reader can write the action of a field theory as a spacetime integral of a Lagrangian density built from fields and their first derivatives, including several fields plus an interaction term.
Reader can derive the field Euler-Lagrange equation by varying fields inside a region with fixed boundary values, integrating by parts and discarding the surface term.
Reader can obtain the wave equation from the string Lagrangian and the Klein-Gordon equation from the free scalar Lagrangian, and read each Lagrangian term as kinetic, gradient or mass energy.
Reader can transfer a flat-space field theory to curved spacetime by inserting sqrt(-g), replacing eta by g and commas by semicolons, and derive the curved-space Klein-Gordon equation.

Reader can explain why varying the metric is harder than varying a matter field (the volume element and all index raising depend on g) and state the three variation rules with their proofs or sources.
Reader can carry out the variation of the Einstein-Hilbert action term by term and show it yields the Einstein tensor, with the Ricci-variation term reducing to a boundary term.
Reader can compute the Hilbert energy-momentum tensor from a matter Lagrangian in both index positions and apply it to a scalar field and the Maxwell field.
Reader can justify the coupling alpha = 16 pi that turns the variational equation into G = 8 pi T in geometrized units.
Reader can derive a Noether current from a symmetry generated by a Killing vector and assemble the canonical energy-momentum tensor from translation symmetry.
Reader can explain why the canonical tensor is generally unsuitable as the source of gravity (non-symmetric, not covariant) and why a symmetric T is linked to angular-momentum conservation.

Reader can set up the Lagrangian description of a perfect fluid (density field, flow-line congruence, conserved current, L = -rho) and follow how the relativistic Euler equation and T = (rho + p) v v + p g emerge.
Reader can state why fluid elements with transverse pressure gradients do not move on geodesics.
Reader can use the geodesic Lagrangian and its Hamiltonian to recover geodesic motion and identify conserved momenta from metric symmetries (exercises).

teaching_approach.summary: A recipe-driven chapter that sells the Lagrangian method as a mechanical procedure: supply the fields, turn the handle, and equations of motion and energy-momentum tensors come out. Every new rule is first run in flat space on a familiar system (string, free scalar), then promoted to curved spacetime by the comma-to-semicolon upgrade. The gravitational part is framed as a toolkit problem: three variation rules are stated and proven or cited before the Einstein-Hilbert algebra is attempted, and T is found by demanding that the combined variation reproduce G = 8 pi T. Noether's theorem is reached geometrically through Lie dragging along Killing fields. The chapter ends with a long, optional, step-numbered fluid derivation borrowed from Hawking and Ellis, explicitly flagged as skippable. Tone is informal; the only justification offered for choosing R as the gravitational Lagrangian is covariance plus the fact that it yields the right field equation.
narrative_arc: Motivation: earlier chapters had to guess T and the field equation; a Lagrangian field theory promises a systematic recipe, and Hilbert found one for gravity in 1915.
Inventory of the fields in play: matter fields (scalar, electromagnetic 1-form, fluid density) that build T, and the metric field g that sets curvature.
Recall particle mechanics (action as time integral of L) and upgrade to fields: Lagrangian density, action as a 4-volume integral, multiple fields plus interaction.
Model systems: string Lagrangian from kinetic and tension energies; free scalar Lagrangian read as kinetic minus gradient minus mass energy.
Formalism: vary the fields in a region with fixed boundary, integrate by parts, drop the surface term, get the field Euler-Lagrange equation.
Checks: wave equation drops out for the string; Klein-Gordon equation for the scalar.
Curved spacetime: sqrt(-g) volume element, covariant derivatives, semicolon form of Euler-Lagrange for scalar and vector fields; curved Klein-Gordon equation.
Gravity: total action S_EH + alpha S_m; explanation that the metric variation changes the measure so it must be done by hand; Hilbert's choice of R as the Lagrangian density.
Toolkit: Rule 1 (variation of inverse metric), Rule 2 (variation of sqrt(-g)), Rule 3 (Palatini identity), with matrix proofs for the first two.
Grind: vary S_EH term by term, reduce the delta R term to a boundary integral, obtain the vacuum Einstein equation.
Energy-momentum tensor: include matter, match to G = 8 pi T, read off T as the metric derivative of the matter Lagrangian, fix alpha = 16 pi, derive the all-down form.
Applications: scalar-field and Maxwell T; remark that gravity itself has no such tensor.
Noether's theorem: drag the Lagrangian along a Killing vector, use Euler-Lagrange to get a conserved current; translations give the canonical energy-momentum tensor, contrasted with the Hilbert one.

Showpiece: perfect fluid as a field theory; vary flow lines by a displacement field while conserving the current, obtain the relativistic Euler equation and, via the Hilbert recipe, the perfect-fluid T.
Summary of three boxed results and exercises extending to Hamiltonian formulations and the symmetry of T.
signature_moves: Field and functional presented as 'machines' with inputs and outputs, and the whole Lagrangian formalism as a machine that outputs T.
Every result first proven in flat space on a concrete system, then promoted to curved spacetime by the comma-to-semicolon rule with the remark that the guessed form is correct.
Toolkit-before-algebra: the three variation rules are isolated, numbered and proven (or cited) before the Einstein-Hilbert variation, whose three terms are then treated in reverse order.
Energy-momentum tensor is not derived from first principles but reverse-engineered: guess the definition that makes the variational equation match G = 8 pi T, then fix alpha.
Physical reading of Lagrangian terms as energy densities (kinetic, gradient cost, cost of existing), checked against T_00.
Noether's theorem phrased with the Part V geometric vocabulary: symmetry means a vanishing Lie derivative of the metric along a Killing field.
Long derivation broken into labelled steps (Step 0 to Step V) with a margin box giving explicit permission to skip it.

sections.title: Chapter opening: why Lagrangians for GR
sections.summary: After a Lagrange epigraph boasting of mechanics without pictures, the chapter pictures a classical field as a device mapping spacetime positions to amplitudes and argues that GR, being a classical field theory, should admit a Lagrangian treatment. The payoff advertised is a systematic, non-ad-hoc route to the energy-momentum tensor and a re-derivation of Einstein's equation, the route Hilbert followed in 1915 just after Einstein. It separates the matter fields (which build T) from the metric field g and promises to couple them through a single Lagrangian.
concepts: matter fields versus the metric field
key_moves: Complains that T was previously assembled by educated guessing, which is unsatisfying given its role as the source of gravity.
Frames the goal: feed fields in, get equations of motion and T out, and recover Einstein's equation.
Splits the fields into matter fields and the single geometric (0,2) field g.

sections.title: Matter fields
sections.summary: Positions GR relative to quantum field theory: particles are excitations of quantized fields, while GR keeps fields classical but starts from the same kind of classical field description. Example 40.1 catalogues the fields to appear: a real scalar, the electromagnetic 1-form gauge field, and the mass-density field of a perfect fluid. Locality is stressed: knowing a field at a point plus its equation of motion lets you predict it elsewhere, and the route to that equation begins with the action.
concepts: quantum field theory picture of particles
key_moves: QFT quantizes classical fields into operators; GR stops at the classical stage.
Lists scalar, 1-form and fluid-density fields as the chapter's cast.
Local field values plus an equation of motion give predictive power, motivating the action.

sections.title: Action and equations of motion
sections.summary: Recalls the particle action as a time integral of L(q, qdot) and upgrades it: L becomes a spatial integral of a Lagrangian density, the action a 4-volume integral of a density depending on the field and its first derivatives. The string (Fig. 40.1, Example 40.2) supplies a concrete density; the free scalar (Example 40.3) supplies the standard relativistic one. Several fields combine additively with an interaction term. Varying the fields in a region with fixed boundary values, integrating by parts and invoking the divergence theorem (Example 40.4) gives the field Euler-Lagrange equation, which reproduces the string wave equation and the Klein-Gordon equation (Examples 40.5, 40.6). A footnote warns that this simple variation assumes the integration measure is independent of the varied field, which fails for the metric.
concepts: principle of stationary action for fields
key_moves: S = integral dt L becomes S = integral d^4x script-L.
String: kinetic energy density from the time derivative of displacement, potential energy density from the slope times tension.
Scalar Lagrangian read as kinetic minus gradient energy minus mass term.
Total action = sum of free actions + interaction action.
Variation: delta(phi_,mu) = (delta phi)_,mu, integrate by parts, surface term vanishes because delta phi = 0 on the boundary, integrand must vanish for arbitrary delta phi.
Apply to string (wave speed sqrt(tension/density)) and to the scalar (Klein-Gordon).

sections.title: Fields in curved spacetime
sections.summary: Promotes the matter-field formalism to curved spacetime: the volume element becomes sqrt(-g) d^4x (footnote derivation from the volume 4-form), partial derivatives become covariant ones, and the Euler-Lagrange equation is written with semicolons for scalars and, component by component, for vector fields. Footnotes remind the reader that derivative indices sit naturally downstairs, so contractions use g^{mu nu}, and that g_{mu nu} = 1/g^{mu nu} only for diagonal metrics. Example 40.7 derives the curved-space Klein-Gordon equation.
key_moves: d^4x -> sqrt(-g) d^4x.
For scalars the gradient needs no connection, so the Lagrangian is unchanged in form.
Guess the covariant Euler-Lagrange equation by replacing partial with covariant derivatives and assert it is right.
Extend to vector components with semicolon notation.
Curved Klein-Gordon: g^{mu nu} phi_{;nu mu} - m^2 phi = 0.

sections.title: Motivating the Einstein equation
sections.summary: Introduces the total action S = S_EH + alpha S_m, where varying matter should give the right-hand side of Einstein's equation and varying geometry the left. Because the varied field is the metric itself, which changes the volume element and index raising, the variation must be done from first principles with respect to g_{mu nu}. Hilbert's Lagrangian density for geometry is the Ricci scalar, stated without proof but motivated by general covariance. Three rules are assembled: the inverse-metric variation with its minus sign (matrix proof, Example 40.8), the determinant variation (log-det identity, Example 40.9), and the Palatini identity (cited). Example 40.10 varies S_EH as three pieces: the sqrt(-g) and inverse-metric variations give -(R^{mu nu} - (1/2) g^{mu nu} R) delta g_{mu nu}, while the delta R_{mu nu} term becomes a total divergence that vanishes on the boundary. The vacuum Einstein equation results.
concepts: variation with respect to the metric
gravitational coupling constant in the action
vacuum Einstein equation from the action
key_moves: Total action = geometry part + alpha times matter part.
Metric variation alters sqrt(-g) d^4x, so no off-the-shelf Euler-Lagrange formula applies.
Choose R as the gravitational Lagrangian density (general covariance, simplest scalar).
Rule 1 from varying M M^-1 = I; Rule 2 from ln det M = Tr ln M; Rule 3 quoted.
Write R = g^{sigma rho} R_{sigma rho} and vary each of sqrt(-g), g^{sigma rho}, R_{sigma rho}.
Index consistency check confirms varying g^{sigma rho} in front of R_{sigma rho}.
Palatini term, using metric compatibility, is a covariant divergence and hence a boundary term.
Remaining integrand gives the Einstein tensor = 0.

sections.title: Energy-momentum tensor
sections.summary: Adds the matter action back in (Example 40.11) and proposes T^{mu nu} = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta(sqrt(-g) L_m)/delta g_{mu nu} so that stationarity of the full action matches Einstein's equation; alpha = 16 pi then gives G = 8 pi T, and the full action is the integral of sqrt(-g)(R + 16 pi L_m). Expanding gives T^{mu nu} = 2 dL_m/dg_{mu nu} + g^{mu nu} L_m, and a footnote converts this to the more convenient T_{mu nu} = -2 dL_m/dg^{mu nu} + g_{mu nu} L_m. Example 40.12 applies it to the scalar field (T_00 is a positive sum of kinetic, gradient and mass energies) and to the Maxwell Lagrangian. The section closes by noting that the gravitational field itself has no energy-momentum tensor.
concepts: gravitational coupling constant in the action
energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
Maxwell Lagrangian and electromagnetic stress tensor
key_moves: Vary total action with respect to g_{mu nu}; geometry gives the Einstein tensor term.
Define T so that the matter part has the same form; set alpha = 16 pi.
Use Rule 2 to expand sqrt(-g) derivative into the g^{mu nu} L_m term.
Chain rule plus Rule 1 converts to derivative with respect to g^{mu nu} and all-down indices.
Scalar: differentiate the single inverse metric; Maxwell: two inverse metrics give a factor 2.
Check T_00 of scalar is a positive energy density.

sections.title: Noether's theorem
sections.summary: States Noether's theorem (continuous symmetry implies conserved current) and derives it by treating the change of the Lagrangian as a Lie derivative along a vector xi, including the metric as a variable. Choosing xi to be a Killing field removes the metric term; using the Euler-Lagrange equation converts the rest into a total divergence, giving the Noether current J_N^alpha = (dL/d(d_alpha phi)) Lie_xi phi - xi^alpha L. Translations in Minkowski space (Example 40.13) give four currents that combine into the canonical energy-momentum tensor S^{alpha beta}, conserved but generally non-symmetric and not suited to curved spacetime, unlike the Hilbert T.
concepts: symmetry of the energy-momentum tensor and angular momentum conservation
key_moves: Write the differential of L including a metric-variation term.
Replace the variation by a Lie derivative along xi; for a scalar Lagrangian it is xi^alpha d_alpha L.
Killing condition kills the metric term.
Substitute Euler-Lagrange for dL/dphi and collect a total divergence.
Translations give S^{alpha beta} with d_alpha S^{alpha beta} = 0.
Contrast S with Hilbert T: equal for scalars (up to convention), different and non-symmetric in general.

sections.title: The perfect fluid
sections.summary: Treats a non-viscous, adiabatic fluid as a field theory with a rest-mass density field and a congruence of timelike flow lines whose normalized tangent is the 4-velocity; the rest-mass current is conserved and the Lagrangian density is minus the total energy density, with pressure p = rho_0^2 du/drho_0. Varying the flow lines by a displacement field K (delta w = Lie_K w) while readjusting rho_0 to keep the current conserved, Example 40.14 (Steps 0-V, after Hawking and Ellis) finds delta rho_0, substitutes it into the action variation and integrates by parts to obtain the relativistic Euler equation (rho + p) vdot = -(g + v v) grad p, showing flow lines are not geodesics when transverse pressure gradients exist. Example 40.15 then finds how rho_0 depends on the metric (holding sqrt(-g) J fixed) and applies the Hilbert prescription to get T = (rho + p) v v + p g.
concepts: flow-line variation by a displacement field
key_moves: Fluid = density field + flow-line congruence; L_m = -rho_0(1 + u).
Vary flow lines via Lie derivative along K, keep J conserved by adjusting rho_0.
Step I-III: vary the conservation law, insert delta v, collect terms proportional to the divergence of v to solve for delta rho_0.
Step IV-V: substitute into delta S, integrate by parts to isolate K_alpha, demand the coefficient vanish.
Identify rho_0 (1 + d(rho_0 u)/d rho_0) = rho + p and rho_0 d_gamma(d(rho_0 u)/d rho_0) = d_gamma p to get Euler's equation.
For T: sqrt(-g) J^alpha is metric-independent, so rho_0^2 = -J.J gives d rho_0/d g_{alpha beta}; insert into the Hilbert recipe.

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Three boxed takeaways: the covariant component form of the Euler-Lagrange equation for matter fields, the Einstein-Hilbert action as the 4-volume integral of the Ricci scalar, and the Hilbert prescription for T^{mu nu} as a metric derivative of the matter Lagrangian plus g^{mu nu} L_m.
key_moves: Condenses the chapter into equations of motion, gravitational action, and energy-momentum recipe.

concepts.name: classical field
concepts.definition: A function on spacetime assigning to each event a value (scalar, vector, 1-form or higher tensor), such as a matter amplitude or the metric, without quantization.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening image: a device fed a spacetime position that returns the field amplitude there; GR is then classified as a classical field theory so the Lagrangian toolkit should apply.

concepts.name: matter fields versus the metric field
aliases: two classes of field in GR
concepts.definition: GR's dynamical content splits into matter fields (scalar fields, the electromagnetic 1-form, fluid density and flow) whose energy content forms T, and the single geometric (0,2) tensor field g that encodes curvature; a Lagrangian formulation must contain and couple both.
concepts.how_introduced: A reminder placed before the formalism, pairing the two sides of Einstein's equation with the two classes of field.

concepts.name: quantum field theory picture of particles
concepts.definition: In quantum field theory each particle species is a quantized excitation of a field; the classical fields are promoted to operators with commutation relations that create and annihilate quanta.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why one starts from classical fields even in GR: QFT begins at the same classical stage and then quantizes, which GR does not do.

concepts.name: real scalar field
concepts.definition: A field phi(x) giving one real number per event; free and with mass parameter m its Lagrangian density (signature -+++) is -(1/2) g^{mu nu} d_mu phi d_nu phi - (1/2) m^2 phi^2, and its quanta are massive spin-0 particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Catalogued in Example 40.1, given its Lagrangian in Example 40.3, and used throughout as the test case for Euler-Lagrange, curved spacetime, T and Noether currents.
concepts.notes: Example 40.1 describes phi(x)^2 as a probability density for finding matter; that reading is not valid for a real relativistic classical field and should not be taught.

concepts.name: electromagnetic gauge 1-form field
concepts.definition: The 1-form field A whose exterior derivative F = dA encodes the electric and magnetic fields; quantized, its excitations are photons.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among matter fields in the opening and Example 40.1, with pointers to ch42 and ch44; its field-strength Lagrangian reappears in Example 40.12.

concepts.name: rest-mass density field
concepts.definition: For a fluid, the scalar field rho_0(x) giving rest mass per unit proper volume in the fluid's rest frame, so that the mass in a small 3-volume is rho_0 times that volume.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in Example 40.1 as the field GR uses most and noted as absent from standard QFT; becomes one of two ingredients of the fluid Lagrangian in 40.7.

concepts.name: action functional
concepts.definition: A functional that assigns a single number (dimensions energy x time) to an entire history of a system: the time integral of the Lagrangian for particles, or the spacetime integral of the Lagrangian density for fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from particle mechanics with N generalized coordinates, then upgraded by turning the Lagrangian into a spatial integral of a density.

concepts.name: Lagrangian density
concepts.definition: A local function of the fields and their first derivatives whose integral over space is the Lagrangian and over spacetime is the action; for simple fields it equals kinetic minus potential energy density.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined through L = integral d^3x script-L, then used as the basic input of field theory; a footnote announces that 'Lagrangian' will mean the density from then on.

concepts.name: Lagrangian of a stretched string
concepts.definition: For a string of linear mass density rho and tension T, transverse displacement psi(x,t) has Lagrangian density (rho/2)(d_t psi)^2 - (T/2)(d_x psi)^2: kinetic energy of motion minus elastic energy stored in the slope.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 40.2 with Fig. 40.1: kinetic and potential energies of a string element written as integrals, then combined into an action whose integrand is the density.

concepts.name: interaction Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The part of the total Lagrangian density containing products of different fields, which couples them; the total action for several fields is the sum of each free action plus the interaction action.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated right after the scalar-field example as the rule for combining two fields phi and psi.

concepts.name: principle of stationary action for fields
concepts.definition: The physically realized field configuration makes the first-order change in the action vanish for every small field variation that is zero on the boundary of the region considered.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from particle mechanics; a footnote cautions that the simple version assumes the volume element does not change when the field is varied, which is exactly what fails for gravity.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equation for fields
aliases: field equation of motion from a Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The partial differential equation dL/dphi = d_mu [dL/d(d_mu phi)] satisfied by any field that makes the action stationary; the particle version's total time derivative becomes a spacetime divergence.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 40.4 by varying inside a region D, using the commutation of variation and differentiation, integrating by parts, discarding the surface term and demanding the integrand vanish.
prerequisites: principle of stationary action for fields

concepts.name: boundary term in the variation
concepts.definition: A total-divergence contribution produced by integration by parts; by the divergence theorem it becomes an integral over the boundary of the region and vanishes when the variation is fixed to zero there.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears in Example 40.4, again in Example 40.10 where the Palatini term reduces to one, and in footnote 21 where a symmetry is allowed to change the action by such a term.

concepts.name: wave equation
concepts.definition: The equation -d_t^2 psi + nabla^2 psi = 0 (unit wave speed), or d_x^2 psi = v^{-2} d_t^2 psi with v = sqrt(tension/density) on a string, describing non-dispersive propagation.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges from the string Lagrangian in Example 40.5; a footnote anticipates metric perturbations obeying it (gravitational waves, ch46).

concepts.name: d'Alembertian operator
concepts.definition: The invariant second-order operator d_mu d^mu = g^{mu nu} d_mu d_nu, equal to -d_t^2 + nabla^2 in Minkowski coordinates with signature (-+++).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as shorthand when writing the wave and Klein-Gordon equations.

concepts.name: Klein-Gordon equation
concepts.definition: The relativistic field equation of a free scalar with mass parameter m: (-d^2 + m^2) phi = 0 in flat spacetime, and g^{mu nu} phi_{;nu mu} - m^2 phi = 0 in curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as the Euler-Lagrange equation of the free scalar Lagrangian in Example 40.6, then re-derived with covariant derivatives in Example 40.7.

concepts.name: invariant volume element
concepts.definition: The coordinate-independent 4-volume element sqrt(-g) d^4x, g being the determinant of the metric components; it is the volume 4-form evaluated on coordinate displacements and makes the action a scalar.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 10 builds it from the volume 4-form; it replaces d^4x in every curved-spacetime action, and its dependence on g is the central complication in varying the metric.

concepts.name: minimal coupling
concepts.definition: The prescription for moving a flat-space field theory into curved spacetime: replace eta by g, partial by covariant derivatives and d^4x by sqrt(-g) d^4x, with no explicit curvature terms added.
concepts.how_introduced: Foreshadowed in footnote 4 (commas become semicolons) and applied in 40.3 by guessing the covariant Euler-Lagrange equation and declaring the guess correct.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name 'minimal coupling' nor mention that the rule is ambiguous in principle (e.g. a term proportional to R phi^2 could be added).

concepts.name: covariant Euler-Lagrange equation
concepts.definition: Curved-spacetime field equations dL/dphi = (dL/dphi_{;mu})_{;mu} for a scalar and dL/dA^nu = (dL/dA^nu_{;mu})_{;mu} for each component of a vector field.
concepts.how_introduced: Guessed from the flat version by the semicolon upgrade in 40.3, extended to vector components, and boxed again in the chapter summary.

concepts.name: Einstein-Hilbert action
concepts.definition: The gravitational action S_EH = integral d^4x sqrt(-g) R, whose Lagrangian density is the Ricci scalar; added to 16 pi times the matter action (G = c = 1) and varied with respect to g_{mu nu}, it yields Einstein's field equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Hilbert's solution to putting geometry into the Lagrangian formalism; justified only by general covariance and simplicity, with success as the real proof.
concepts.notes: The boundary (Gibbons-Hawking-York) term needed for a well-posed variation is not discussed.

concepts.name: variation with respect to the metric
concepts.definition: Computing the change in an action under a small change delta g_{mu nu} of the metric components; since g also enters sqrt(-g), every raised index and the connection, it must be carried out explicitly rather than by quoting the matter-field Euler-Lagrange formula.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated in 40.4 by the observation that changing g changes the spacetime intervals and the volume element itself.
concepts.notes: The book insists on varying g_{mu nu} rather than g^{mu nu}; in fact both give equivalent equations because the two variations are related by Rule 1.

concepts.name: gravitational coupling constant in the action
concepts.definition: The relative weight alpha between gravitational and matter actions; with G = c = 1 and T defined by the Hilbert prescription, alpha = 16 pi makes the variational equation read G_{mu nu} = 8 pi T_{mu nu} (in SI the gravitational term carries c^4/(16 pi G)).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an undetermined constant in S = S_EH + alpha S_m, fixed in Example 40.11 by matching to Einstein's equation.

concepts.name: variation of the inverse metric
concepts.definition: delta g^{sigma rho} = -g^{sigma mu} g^{rho nu} delta g_{mu nu}: because g^{mu alpha} g_{alpha nu} = delta^mu_nu is fixed, the variation of the inverse picks up a minus sign and two inverse metrics.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the first of three tricks and proven in Example 40.8 by varying the matrix identity M M^-1 = I.

concepts.name: variation of the metric determinant
concepts.definition: delta sqrt(-g) = (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^{mu nu} delta g_{mu nu}, which follows from delta(det M) = det M Tr(M^{-1} delta M).
concepts.how_introduced: Second trick; proven in Example 40.9 from the log-determinant identity.

concepts.name: log-determinant identity
aliases: ln det M = Tr ln M
concepts.definition: For an invertible matrix, the log of the determinant equals the trace of the matrix logarithm (both are the sum of log-eigenvalues), so delta ln det M = Tr(M^{-1} delta M).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted with proof deferred to an exercise or to ch34 Exercise 34.3; used in Example 40.9.

concepts.name: Palatini identity
concepts.definition: delta R_{alpha beta} = nabla_mu(delta Gamma^mu_{alpha beta}) - nabla_beta(delta Gamma^mu_{alpha mu}): the first-order change in the Ricci tensor is built from covariant derivatives of the (tensorial) change in the connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Third trick, quoted without derivation (reference to Zee 2013), then used in Example 40.10 to turn the Ricci-variation term into a boundary integral.

concepts.name: tensor character of connection variations
concepts.definition: The Christoffel symbols are not tensor components, but the difference of two connections, and hence an infinitesimal variation delta Gamma, transforms as a (1,2) tensor, so its covariant derivatives are meaningful.
concepts.how_introduced: Credited to Palatini in a biographical footnote.

concepts.name: vacuum Einstein equation from the action
concepts.definition: Stationarity of the Einstein-Hilbert action alone gives R^{mu nu} - (1/2) g^{mu nu} R = 0, the field equation of spacetime without matter (equivalent to R_{mu nu} = 0 in four dimensions).
concepts.how_introduced: Conclusion of Example 40.10 after the three variation rules are applied.
concepts.notes: Vacuum does not mean flat: Schwarzschild and gravitational waves solve this equation.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric, divergence-free tensor G^{mu nu} = R^{mu nu} - (1/2) g^{mu nu} R forming the geometric side of Einstein's equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Here it emerges automatically from the metric variation of sqrt(-g) R, rather than being engineered for conservation as in ch13.

concepts.name: Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: G_{mu nu} = 8 pi T_{mu nu} in geometrized units: the condition that the total action integral sqrt(-g)(R + 16 pi L_m) be stationary under metric variations.
concepts.how_introduced: Recovered in Example 40.11 by combining the Einstein-Hilbert variation with the matter variation.

concepts.name: Hilbert energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: T^{mu nu} = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta(sqrt(-g) L_m)/delta g_{mu nu} = 2 dL_m/dg_{mu nu} + g^{mu nu} L_m, equivalently T_{mu nu} = -2 dL_m/dg^{mu nu} + g_{mu nu} L_m: the response of the matter Lagrangian to a change of the metric, symmetric by construction and automatically covariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Reverse-engineered in Example 40.11 by requiring the matter variation to supply the right-hand side of Einstein's equation; the all-down version follows in footnote 19 by the chain rule and Rule 1.
prerequisites: variation with respect to the metric

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
concepts.definition: T_{mu nu} = d_mu phi d_nu phi - g_{mu nu}[(1/2) g^{alpha beta} d_alpha phi d_beta phi + (1/2) m^2 phi^2]; in flat space T_00 = (1/2) phidot^2 + (1/2)(grad phi)^2 + (1/2) m^2 phi^2, a positive energy density.
concepts.how_introduced: First application of the Hilbert prescription (Example 40.12): only one inverse metric appears in the Lagrangian, so the derivative is immediate.

concepts.name: Maxwell Lagrangian and electromagnetic stress tensor
concepts.definition: The electromagnetic Lagrangian is minus one quarter of the Faraday tensor fully contracted with itself through two inverse metrics; the Hilbert recipe turns it into a symmetric, traceless stress tensor made of F contracted with F on one index, minus a quarter of the metric times the invariant F-squared (Heaviside-Lorentz-type normalization).
concepts.how_introduced: Second part of Example 40.12, with a pointer to ch42; the two inverse metrics in the contraction produce the factor that cancels the 1/4.

concepts.name: non-localizability of gravitational energy
concepts.definition: General relativity supplies no local, covariant energy-momentum tensor for the gravitational field itself; just as there is no gravitational force, gravitational energy cannot be assigned point by point.
concepts.how_introduced: One-paragraph remark closing 40.5 after the matter-field examples.

concepts.name: Noether's theorem
concepts.definition: Each continuous symmetry of an action (a transformation leaving it unchanged up to a boundary term) implies a current with vanishing divergence, and hence a conserved quantity.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in 40.6 by dragging the Lagrangian along a vector field, treating the change as a Lie derivative, choosing a Killing field to remove the metric term and using the Euler-Lagrange equation.

concepts.name: continuous symmetry of the action
concepts.definition: A continuous family of transformations of the fields and coordinates under which the action is unchanged, possibly up to a surface term.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in 40.6 as the input to Noether's theorem; the footnote allows a surface-term change.

concepts.name: Lie derivative
concepts.definition: The derivative measuring how a tensor field changes when transported along the flow of a vector field; acting on a scalar it is simply the directional derivative along that vector, and acting on a vector it is the commutator of the two fields, which can be written with covariant derivatives because the connection terms cancel.
concepts.how_introduced: Used twice: as the variation of the Lagrangian under a symmetry in 40.6, and as the change in the flow-line tangent under a displacement field in 40.7.

concepts.name: Killing vector field
concepts.definition: A vector field along which the metric does not change, Lie_xi g = 0; in Minkowski space the constant translations (and Lorentz generators) are examples.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Part V as the geometric expression of symmetry; choosing xi Killing removes the metric-variation term in the Noether derivation.

concepts.name: Noether current
concepts.definition: For a symmetry generated by a Killing vector xi acting on a scalar field, J_N^alpha = [dL/d(d_alpha phi)] Lie_xi phi - xi^alpha L, whose divergence vanishes on solutions.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the bracket in the conservation equation derived in 40.6; specialized to an x-translation in Example 40.13.

concepts.name: canonical energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: S^{alpha beta} = [dL/d(d_alpha phi)] d^beta phi - g^{alpha beta} L, the four Noether currents of spacetime translations stacked together, obeying d_alpha S^{alpha beta} = 0; in general it is neither symmetric nor defined covariantly in curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled after Example 40.13 and contrasted with the Hilbert tensor as unsuitable for Einstein's equation.
concepts.notes: With the book's scalar Lagrangian and signature, S^{alpha beta} as written equals minus the Hilbert T^{alpha beta}; the book says they are 'the same', which holds only up to this overall sign convention.

concepts.name: symmetry of the energy-momentum tensor and angular momentum conservation
concepts.definition: In flat spacetime the angular-momentum flux, formed by multiplying position with the energy-momentum tensor and antisymmetrizing, has zero divergence only when the energy-momentum tensor is symmetric in its two indices; a symmetric source is therefore required.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed to in footnote 24 and turned into Exercise 40.4.

concepts.name: perfect fluid (field-theoretic description)
concepts.definition: A viscosity-free, adiabatic fluid described by a rest-mass density field and a congruence of timelike flow lines, with conserved rest-mass current and Lagrangian density equal to minus its total energy density, L_m = -rho_0(1 + u).
concepts.how_introduced: Opens 40.7 by recasting ch39's fluid as two fields; the Lagrangian is then varied in two ways, by moving flow lines (equation of motion) and by changing the metric (T).

concepts.name: flow-line congruence and fluid 4-velocity
concepts.definition: A family of non-crossing timelike curves filling spacetime, one per fluid element; the tangent w = d/dtau normalized as v = w/sqrt(-g(w,w)) is the 4-velocity with g(v,v) = -1.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the second ingredient of the fluid field theory.

concepts.name: rest-mass current conservation
concepts.definition: The current J = rho_0 v has zero covariant divergence, equivalently d_alpha(sqrt(-g) J^alpha) = 0: rest mass is neither created nor destroyed along the flow.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed as a constraint that is preserved while flow lines are varied; its divergence form with sqrt(-g) is used to get the metric dependence of rho_0.

concepts.name: specific internal energy and pressure
concepts.definition: u is internal energy per unit rest mass, a function of rho_0 for adiabatic flow; the first law then gives pressure p = rho_0^2 du/drho_0, and total energy density rho = rho_0(1 + u).
concepts.how_introduced: Given in the fluid Lagrangian and footnote 25; it is the identity that turns derivatives of rho_0 u into rho + p and grad p.

concepts.name: flow-line variation by a displacement field
concepts.definition: The fluid action is varied by shifting points of each flow line by a vector field K; the tangent changes by the Lie derivative of w along K, and rho_0 is simultaneously adjusted to keep the current conserved.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the fluid analogue of varying a field; its consequences are worked out in Steps I-III of Example 40.14.

concepts.name: relativistic Euler equation
concepts.definition: (rho + p) v^alpha_{;beta} v^beta = -(g^{alpha beta} + v^alpha v^beta) p_{,beta}: a perfect fluid's flow lines accelerate in response to the pressure gradient projected orthogonal to the flow, with inertia set by rho + p.
concepts.how_introduced: Final result of Example 40.14; matched to eqn 39.77 of the previous chapter.

concepts.name: projection tensor orthogonal to 4-velocity
concepts.definition: h^{alpha beta} = g^{alpha beta} + v^alpha v^beta projects any vector onto the 3-space orthogonal to v (the fluid's local rest space).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears unnamed in the Euler equation and in d rho_0/d g_{alpha beta}.

concepts.name: non-geodesic motion of fluid elements
concepts.definition: Fluid elements do not follow geodesics (v-dot is nonzero) whenever pressure varies across the flow; only pressureless dust moves geodesically.
concepts.how_introduced: Promised in footnote 27 and confirmed after the Euler equation is obtained.

concepts.name: densitized current
concepts.definition: The combination sqrt(-g) J^alpha, whose ordinary divergence is sqrt(-g) times the covariant divergence of J; it is held fixed when the metric is varied, which fixes how rho_0 depends on g.
concepts.how_introduced: The 'trick' of Example 40.15 that exposes the metric dependence of the density.

concepts.name: perfect fluid energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The stress-energy of a perfect fluid: the enthalpy density (energy density plus pressure) times the outer product of the 4-velocity with itself, plus pressure times the inverse metric; in this chapter it is obtained from the fluid Lagrangian via the Hilbert prescription.
concepts.how_introduced: Outcome of Example 40.15, confirming the form guessed physically in ch12 and ch39.

concepts.name: geodesic Lagrangian for a particle
concepts.definition: The particle Lagrangian L = (1/2) g_{mu nu} xdot^mu xdot^nu with proper-time derivatives; its Euler-Lagrange equations are the geodesic equation, and coordinates absent from the metric yield conserved momenta (p_t, p_phi in Schwarzschild).
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 40.1 and 40.2 use it to connect the chapter back to particle motion.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian and Hamiltonian density
concepts.definition: Legendre transforms of the Lagrangian: H = p_mu xdot^mu - L with p_mu = dL/dxdot^mu for particles (H = (1/2) g^{mu nu} p_mu p_nu for the geodesic Lagrangian), and script-H = pi phidot - script-L with pi = dL/dphidot for fields, leading to first-order Hamilton's equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 40.1 and 40.3 build them by analogy with the particle case.

figures.label: Fig. 40.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A string displaced from equilibrium by psi(x,t); a short element of length dx and mass rho dx is singled out to set up the equation of motion. Only a middle portion of a string tied at both ends is drawn.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn line sketch of a thick, tube-like string seen slightly in perspective, cut off at both ends (the tied endpoints are off the picture). It rises from the left to a crest, falls through the axis and dips into a trough on the right, so a little under one full wavelength is shown. A dashed horizontal line marks equilibrium. From the point labelled x on that line, a vertical arrow climbs to the string and is labelled psi(x,t). Just past the crest, on the downslope, a narrow slice of the string is shaded; two short tick arrows above it mark its width dx and the label rho dx sits beside it. Small strokes next to the string hint at its transverse motion.
figures.what_it_teaches: Gives the continuum picture behind a Lagrangian density: each small element carries kinetic energy from its vertical motion and potential energy from the string's slope, so the Lagrangian becomes an integral over x of a local density.

redesign.idea: Beads-to-continuum string: start with a handful of point masses joined by springs, each showing its own kinetic and spring energy, then refine the number of beads until the chain becomes the smooth string of the figure; under it, two colored strips plot the kinetic density (rho/2) psi_t^2 and gradient density (T/2) psi_x^2 along x, and a readout integrates their difference into L and the running action.
redesign.interaction: Learner plucks or drags the string into any shape, adjusts tension and linear density, and toggles between 'free evolution' and 'try a wrong motion'; the wrong-motion mode perturbs the true solution with a bump vanishing at fixed endpoints and shows the action changing only at second order, while wave speed sqrt(T/rho) updates.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.1
worked_examples.problem: Catalogue the kinds of classical field the chapter will use.
worked_examples.method: Describe what each field takes in and returns: a real scalar, a vector or 1-form (the electromagnetic potential), and the perfect-fluid density.
worked_examples.key_insight: Fields differ in the type of value they output at each event; the fluid density is the field GR uses most but is not standard in QFT.
worked_examples.result: Scalar field (spin-0 quanta), electromagnetic 1-form (photons), fluid mass-density field.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.2
worked_examples.problem: Write the action and Lagrangian density for transverse waves on a string of given density and tension.
worked_examples.method: Integrate kinetic energy density of the moving element and potential energy density from stretching (proportional to slope squared) along the string, form T - V and integrate in time.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Lagrangian of a continuous system is an integral of a local density depending on the field's time and space derivatives.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.3
worked_examples.problem: Interpret the free scalar field Lagrangian.
worked_examples.method: Expand the contraction with the Minkowski metric and read each term physically.
worked_examples.key_insight: The three terms are the energy of change in time, the cost of spatial variation, and a cost for the field having any nonzero value.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.4
worked_examples.problem: Derive the field Euler-Lagrange equation from stationarity of the action in flat spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Vary phi inside a region D with delta phi = 0 on its boundary; commute variation and derivative; integrate by parts; convert the total divergence to a boundary integral that vanishes; require the remaining integrand to vanish for arbitrary delta phi.
worked_examples.key_insight: The time derivative of the particle Euler-Lagrange equation becomes a spacetime divergence, and the boundary condition on the variation is what kills the surface term.
concepts: principle of stationary action for fields

worked_examples.label: Example 40.5
worked_examples.problem: Find the equation of motion of the string.
worked_examples.method: Apply the field Euler-Lagrange equation with derivatives with respect to psi_x and psi_t.
worked_examples.key_insight: The wave equation and wave speed follow with essentially no physics input beyond the energies.
worked_examples.result: T psi_xx = rho psi_tt, wave speed v = sqrt(T/rho).

worked_examples.label: Example 40.6
worked_examples.problem: Find the equation of motion of the free scalar field in Minkowski space.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the Lagrangian with respect to phi and d_mu phi, substitute into the Euler-Lagrange equation.
worked_examples.key_insight: A relativistic wave equation with a mass term, the Klein-Gordon equation, emerges.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.7
worked_examples.problem: Derive the scalar field equation in curved spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Write the Lagrangian with covariant derivatives and g^{mu nu}; differentiate with respect to phi_{;mu}; take the covariant divergence using metric compatibility.
worked_examples.key_insight: The flat recipe carries over unchanged once commas become semicolons and the metric is kept explicit.
worked_examples.result: g^{mu nu} phi_{;nu mu} - m^2 phi = 0.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.8
worked_examples.problem: Prove the rule for varying the inverse metric (Rule 1).
worked_examples.method: Vary the matrix identity M M^-1 = I, solve for delta(M^-1), and identify M with g_{mu nu}.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because the product with the inverse is fixed, the inverse must change oppositely: the essential minus sign.
worked_examples.result: delta g^{alpha delta} = -g^{alpha beta} delta g_{beta gamma} g^{gamma delta}.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.9
worked_examples.problem: Prove the rule for varying sqrt(-g) (Rule 2).
worked_examples.method: Differentiate ln det M = Tr ln M to get delta det M = det M Tr(M^-1 delta M), then insert the metric and take the square root.
worked_examples.key_insight: The determinant responds to a change in the matrix through the trace of M^-1 delta M.
worked_examples.result: delta sqrt(-g) = (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^{mu nu} delta g_{mu nu}.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.10
worked_examples.problem: Vary the Einstein-Hilbert action with respect to the metric.
worked_examples.method: Write R = g^{sigma rho} R_{sigma rho}; split the variation into delta R, delta g^{sigma rho} and delta sqrt(-g) pieces; treat them in reverse order with Rule 2 and Rule 1; use the Palatini identity and metric compatibility to write the delta R piece as a covariant divergence; discard it as a boundary term.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the variations of the metric in the measure and in the contraction contribute; the curvature variation is a pure boundary term, and the survivors assemble into the Einstein tensor.
worked_examples.result: delta S_EH = -integral sqrt(-g) (R^{mu nu} - (1/2) g^{mu nu} R) delta g_{mu nu}, so G^{mu nu} = 0 in vacuum.
concepts: vacuum Einstein equation from the action

worked_examples.label: Example 40.11
worked_examples.problem: Obtain the energy-momentum tensor and Einstein's equation from the combined gravity-plus-matter action.
worked_examples.method: Vary S_EH + alpha S_m with respect to g_{mu nu}; use the previous result for the geometric part; choose T^{mu nu} as 2/sqrt(-g) times the metric derivative of sqrt(-g) L_m so both terms have the same form; fix alpha.
worked_examples.key_insight: T is whatever quantity the matter Lagrangian contributes when the metric is varied; the normalization 16 pi is set purely by matching to G = 8 pi T.
worked_examples.result: alpha = 16 pi; S = integral sqrt(-g)(R + 16 pi L_m); T^{mu nu} = 2 dL_m/dg_{mu nu} + g^{mu nu} L_m.
concepts: gravitational coupling constant in the action

worked_examples.label: Example 40.12
worked_examples.problem: Compute the energy-momentum tensors of a scalar field and of the electromagnetic field.
worked_examples.method: Apply T_{mu nu} = -2 dL_m/dg^{mu nu} + g_{mu nu} L_m, noting one inverse metric in the scalar Lagrangian and two in the Maxwell Lagrangian; check the scalar T_00 in flat space.
worked_examples.key_insight: The recipe works mechanically; the positive T_00 confirms physical sense.
worked_examples.result: Scalar: T = d phi d phi - g[(1/2)(d phi)^2 + (1/2) m^2 phi^2], T_00 = (1/2)phidot^2 + (1/2)(grad phi)^2 + (1/2) m^2 phi^2. EM: T = F F g - (1/4) g F F.
concepts: energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field
Maxwell Lagrangian and electromagnetic stress tensor

worked_examples.label: Example 40.13
worked_examples.problem: Find the Noether current for translations in x.
worked_examples.method: Take xi = e_x, which is Killing in Minkowski space, so Lie_xi phi = d_x phi, and insert into the Noether current formula.
worked_examples.key_insight: Translation invariance yields momentum-type currents; the four translations together form the canonical energy-momentum tensor.
worked_examples.result: J_N^alpha = [dL/d(d_alpha phi)] d_x phi - delta^alpha_x L; combined: S^{alpha beta} with d_alpha S^{alpha beta} = 0.

worked_examples.label: Example 40.14
worked_examples.problem: Derive the relativistic Euler equation of a perfect fluid from its Lagrangian.
worked_examples.method: Step 0: write delta S in terms of delta rho_0. Step I: vary the conservation law. Step II: express delta v via the Lie derivative of w along the displacement K and the normalization. Step III: substitute, integrate along flow lines, collect terms with the divergence of v to solve for delta rho_0. Step IV: substitute into delta S. Step V: integrate by parts to isolate K_alpha and set its coefficient to zero, then use p = rho_0^2 du/drho_0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Treating the flow lines as the varied field (with mass conservation enforced) turns a fluid into a field theory; the Euler equation and non-geodesic motion drop out of stationarity.
concepts: flow-line variation by a displacement field

worked_examples.label: Example 40.15
worked_examples.problem: Derive the perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor from the fluid Lagrangian.
worked_examples.method: Note the metric enters only through rho_0; hold the densitized current sqrt(-g) J fixed (from the determinant form of the divergence); write rho_0^2 as minus J.J and vary it with respect to g_{alpha beta} using Rule 2; insert into the Hilbert recipe and identify rho and p.
worked_examples.key_insight: The metric dependence of the density is fixed by particle-number conservation, and pressure appears through du/drho_0.
worked_examples.result: T^{alpha beta} = (rho + p) v^alpha v^beta + p g^{alpha beta}.

worked_examples.problem: Derive Noether's theorem for a scalar field in Minkowski space using a Killing vector.
worked_examples.method: Write the differential of L including a metric term; replace variations by Lie derivatives along xi; the Killing condition removes the metric term; replace dL/dphi with the Euler-Lagrange expression; recognize a total divergence.
worked_examples.key_insight: Symmetry is geometric (vanishing Lie derivative of the metric) and conservation follows from on-shell rearrangement into a divergence.
worked_examples.result: d_alpha[(dL/d(d_alpha phi)) Lie_xi phi - xi^alpha L] = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Convert the Hilbert prescription to the all-down form with derivatives with respect to g^{mu nu} (footnote 19).
worked_examples.method: Chain rule for d/dg_{mu nu} via g^{alpha beta}, insert Rule 1, then lower both indices with the metric and contract Kronecker deltas.
worked_examples.key_insight: Raising or lowering what you differentiate with respect to flips the sign of the derivative term.
worked_examples.result: T_{mu nu} = -2 dL_m/dg^{mu nu} + g_{mu nu} L_m.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A field is a machine: put in a spacetime position, get out an amplitude.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Opens the chapter and 40.1 so that fields feel like concrete functions rather than abstractions.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Says nothing about what type of value comes out or how it transforms; the metric field is also such a machine but plays a very different role.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Probe tool: click any event on a spacetime grid and see the value of a scalar field, a vector, or a metric ellipse displayed there.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lagrangian field theory as a turn-the-handle machine: feed in matter fields and a Lagrangian, and the equations of motion and T(x) come out.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates the chapter against earlier ad-hoc constructions of T.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The machine still needs a guessed Lagrangian (and the choice of R for gravity is not derived); the output T depends on conventions.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Pipeline widget: drop a Lagrangian card (scalar, Maxwell, fluid) into a hopper and watch symbolic output cards for the field equation and T appear step by step.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Dictionary from particle mechanics to fields: coordinates q_i become field values phi(x), the discrete index i becomes the continuous position, sums become integrals, and the Lagrangian becomes a spatial integral of a density.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used to upgrade the particle action and Euler-Lagrange equation to fields with maximal resemblance.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Fields have spatial derivatives with no particle analogue, which is where the divergence in the field equation comes from.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Beads-to-string morph: a chain of N coupled beads with its discrete Lagrangian continuously refines into a string as N grows, with the sum turning into an integral on screen.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Terms in the scalar Lagrangian as energy costs: time variation is kinetic energy, spatial variation costs gradient energy, and the mass term is a cost for the field existing at all.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Read directly off the Minkowski form and later checked by the positive T_00.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Energy is T_00 (a sum), whereas the Lagrangian is a difference; the 'cost of existing' picture fails for potentials with negative curvature (e.g. inflaton or Higgs-like potentials).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Three sliders scale a wave packet's frequency, wavelength and amplitude; bar gauges show kinetic, gradient and mass contributions to both L and T_00.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Dragging the Lagrangian along a vector and comparing with the original, as a way to test for symmetry.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The variation under a symmetry is recast as a Lie derivative along xi.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only symmetries generated by vector fields (spacetime symmetries) fit this picture; internal symmetries like phase rotations need a different variation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flow-field overlay: a Minkowski grid with a translation or boost Killing field; dragging a field configuration along it leaves the action unchanged, and a flux counter shows the Noether current through a box staying balanced.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Integrating along flow lines 'undoes' covariant derivatives, like integrating a derivative along a curve.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: flow-line variation by a displacement field
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used in Step III of Example 40.14 to justify moving semicolons by integration by parts.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only derivatives along the flow direction are directional derivatives along the lines; the contracted indices in the fluid derivation are not all along the flow, so the picture is heuristic.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Varying the metric changes the ruler with which the action is measured.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: variation with respect to the metric
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why metric variation needs special care: it alters intervals and the volume element sqrt(-g) d^4x.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Metaphor does not by itself tell you the rules; the three explicit variation identities do the work.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Deformable grid: stretch a patch of a 2D metric and watch the area element and the integral of a fixed field over the patch change, contrasting with varying the field on a fixed grid.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity can be handled like any matter field: write a Lagrangian and plug it into the standard Euler-Lagrange formula.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The varied field is the metric, which also sits in the volume element and in every index contraction, so the variation must be done explicitly with the rules for delta g^{mu nu}, delta sqrt(-g) and delta R_{mu nu}.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The matter-field recipe worked so smoothly for strings and scalars.
concepts: variation with respect to the metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Raising the indices of a variation is as harmless as raising indices of a tensor: delta g^{mu nu} = g^{mu alpha} g^{nu beta} delta g_{alpha beta}.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: There is an extra minus sign, delta g^{mu nu} = -g^{mu alpha} g^{nu beta} delta g_{alpha beta}, because the inverse must compensate a change in the matrix.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Index gymnastics usually carries no signs.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The component g_{mu nu} is simply 1/g^{mu nu}.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only for a diagonal metric; in general g^{mu nu} is the matrix inverse.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Most metrics met so far (Schwarzschild, FRW) are diagonal.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The gravitational field carries a local energy-momentum tensor just like the electromagnetic field.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: GR gives no covariant local energy density for gravity; the Hilbert recipe applies to matter fields only.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Gravitational waves transport energy, and every other field has a T.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Noether energy-momentum tensor from translation symmetry is the tensor that sources Einstein's equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The canonical tensor is generally non-symmetric and not generally covariant; the symmetric Hilbert tensor from metric variation is the correct source (they coincide, up to sign convention, for a scalar field).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are conserved and both are called energy-momentum tensors.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every element of a fluid falls freely along a geodesic.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Pressure gradients orthogonal to the flow accelerate fluid elements; only pressureless dust moves geodesically.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The equivalence principle is often summarized as 'everything follows geodesics'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Varying the action with respect to g^{mu nu} instead of g_{mu nu} would give a different or wrong field equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The two variations are related by Rule 1, so the resulting equations are equivalent (one is the other with indices lowered); the choice is a matter of convenience, and the book itself uses g^{mu nu} derivatives for T_{mu nu}.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book states it is important to vary g_{mu nu} because the metric is naturally a (0,2) tensor.
concepts: variation with respect to the metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The vacuum equation G = 0 means no gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Vacuum means no matter source; curvature can still be present, as in Schwarzschild spacetime or gravitational waves.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book calls it a 'stripped-down' Einstein equation, suggesting something trivial.
concepts: vacuum Einstein equation from the action

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A real classical scalar field phi describes the probability of finding a particle, with phi^2 as a probability density.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A real relativistic field has no positive-definite conserved probability density; its physical content is its energy-momentum. Probability interpretations belong to quantum states, not classical field amplitudes.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Non-relativistic wavefunction language is familiar, and Example 40.1 phrases the scalar field this way.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The action is kinetic energy minus potential energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Lagrangian is kinetic minus potential energy; the action is its integral over time (or the density's integral over spacetime).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book itself makes this slip in a sentence in 40.2.

thought_experiments.name: Wiggling a field inside a box with clamped walls
thought_experiments.setup: Change the field by a small amount only inside a finite spacetime region, keeping it fixed on the region's boundary, and ask how the action changes.
thought_experiments.lesson: Requiring no first-order change for every such wiggle is equivalent to the local Euler-Lagrange equation; the clamped boundary is what removes the surface term.
concepts: principle of stationary action for fields
thought_experiments.app_idea: Heat-map of a 1+1D field with a draggable rectangular region; learner paints a bump variation inside it and a gauge shows delta S, which is zero to first order only for the true solution.

thought_experiments.name: Varying the metric instead of the field
thought_experiments.setup: Keep all matter fields fixed but deform the metric slightly inside a region, so distances, volumes and index contractions change.
thought_experiments.lesson: The response of geometry gives the Einstein tensor and the response of matter defines T; balancing them is Einstein's equation.
concepts: variation with respect to the metric
thought_experiments.app_idea: 2D grid with a metric-ellipse at each point; learner stretches the metric locally and two meters show the change in the integral of R and the change in the matter action.

thought_experiments.name: Sliding a field configuration along a symmetry
thought_experiments.setup: Translate a solution of the scalar field equation along a Killing direction of Minkowski space and compare the Lagrangian before and after.
thought_experiments.lesson: Because the metric is unchanged by the slide, the action is unchanged, and on solutions this forces a conserved current (momentum or energy).
thought_experiments.app_idea: Wave packet in a box with a translation handle; a flux meter at the box walls shows momentum entering equals momentum change inside.

thought_experiments.name: Nudging the flow lines of a fluid
thought_experiments.setup: Displace every point of every flow line of a perfect fluid by a vector field K while re-adjusting the density so no mass is created or destroyed.
thought_experiments.lesson: Stationarity of the fluid action under such nudges produces the relativistic Euler equation, and the density must change by the divergence-like expression in eqn 40.89.
concepts: flow-line variation by a displacement field
thought_experiments.app_idea: Streamline plot of a 2D flow with a brush that applies a displacement field K; streamlines deform, density shading updates to keep flux through a moving box constant, and an action meter responds.

historical_notes.event: Hilbert found a variational (action-based) derivation of the gravitational field equations, now the Einstein-Hilbert action, just after Einstein reached the field equations by a less systematic route.
historical_notes.significance: Shows two complementary routes to GR: physical reasoning (Einstein) and an action principle (Hilbert), the latter being the template for modern field theory.

historical_notes.event: Hilbert presented a list of mathematical problems that shaped twentieth-century research.
Einstein developed GR over eight years; Ohanian and Ruffini remark that the theory arrived about two decades before the relativistic gauge-field methods that make it natural had matured.
historical_notes.significance: Frames this chapter's field-theory methods as the natural modern language of GR; points to Pais and Cheng for the history.

historical_notes.event: Epigraph from Mecanique Analytique, in which Lagrange boasts that his mechanics needs no figures, only uniform algebraic procedure.
historical_notes.significance: Sets the tone of the chapter: a mechanical, algebraic recipe rather than geometric pictures (ironic in a book that elsewhere relies on diagrams).

historical_notes.event: Showed that variations of the connection coefficients are components of a tensor, leading to the identity for the variation of the Ricci tensor that bears his name.
historical_notes.significance: Makes the Einstein-Hilbert variation tractable by reducing the curvature variation to a boundary term.

historical_notes.event: Noether's theorem linking continuous symmetries to conservation laws (named in 40.6 with dates 1882-1935).
historical_notes.significance: Underlies energy, momentum and angular momentum conservation and the canonical energy-momentum tensor.

historical_notes.event: Their variational derivation of perfect-fluid dynamics is the model for Example 40.14, with steps they omitted filled in.
historical_notes.significance: Credits the source of the chapter's most technical derivation.

applications_and_observations.details: The string Lagrangian yields waves with speed sqrt(tension/linear density). Own estimate for a guitar-like string: tension 70 N and 5 g/m give about 120 m/s.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: v = sqrt(T/rho); own estimate: T = 70 N, rho = 5e-3 kg/m, v approx 118 m/s

applications_and_observations.topic: Gravitational waves obey a wave equation
applications_and_observations.details: A footnote previews that excitations of the metric field satisfy the unit-speed wave equation, developed in ch46.

The scalar-field Lagrangian and its energy-momentum tensor are advertised as the tools for symmetry breaking and inflation in ch41; T_00 = kinetic + gradient + potential energy is the ingredient that drives cosmic expansion.

applications_and_observations.topic: Stars and cosmological fluids as perfect fluids
applications_and_observations.details: The Lagrangian perfect fluid reproduces the relativistic Euler equation and T = (rho + p) v v + p g used for stellar interiors and Friedmann cosmology; pressure contributes to inertia through rho + p.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: in a neutron-star core p/rho can reach a few tenths, so pressure inertia is not negligible; in the Sun p/rho is of order 1e-6.

applications_and_observations.topic: Normalization of the gravitational action in SI units
applications_and_observations.details: The book's alpha = 16 pi with G = c = 1 corresponds in SI units to a gravitational action (c^4/16 pi G) integral sqrt(-g) R plus the matter action (own conversion).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: c^4/(16 pi G) approx 2.4e42 N (own estimate)

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-,+,+,+): the free scalar Lagrangian -(1/2)(d phi)^2 gives +(1/2)phidot^2 - (1/2)(grad phi)^2, and fluid velocity satisfies g(v,v) = -1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Particle physics texts with (+,-,-,-) flip the sign of the kinetic term and of the Hilbert T formula.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized units G = c = 1, so the coupling in the action is 16 pi and Einstein's equation reads G = 8 pi T.
A comma before an index marks a partial derivative and a semicolon a covariant derivative; for vector components the connection term is added for an upper index and subtracted for a lower index.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The chapter's slogan: commas become semicolons in curved spacetime.

notation_and_conventions.item: Order of indices on second covariant derivatives
notation_and_conventions.convention: Footnote 13 writes phi_{;mu nu} = (d_nu phi)_{;mu}, i.e. the last index is differentiated first, the opposite of the common convention (phi_{;mu})_{;nu}.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Irrelevant for scalars on a torsion-free connection, but a trap for vectors.

notation_and_conventions.convention: script-L_m matter density, script-L_EH geometric density (= R), script-L_int interaction; 'Lagrangian' means density from 40.2 onward.
A script L with subscript vector (printed like a pound sign), e.g. Lie_xi phi, Lie_K w.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Visually close to the Lagrangian density symbol; watch context in eqns 40.68-40.72.

notation_and_conventions.convention: S denotes both the action and the canonical energy-momentum tensor S^{alpha beta}.
delta/delta g_{mu nu} and partial d/dg_{mu nu} are used interchangeably for the metric derivative of the Lagrangian density; no functional-derivative subtleties are tracked.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Valid when L_m depends on g but not on its derivatives, as for all examples here.

notation_and_conventions.convention: g = det g_{mu nu}, negative in Lorentzian signature; the volume element is sqrt(-g) d^4x.
R_{nu beta} = R^mu_{nu mu beta}, contracting the first and third Riemann indices; R = g^{alpha beta} R_{alpha beta}.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Consistent with ch11; other books contract differently and change signs.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Book-specific labels: Rule 1 inverse-metric variation (40.37), Rule 2 determinant variation (40.41), Rule 3 Palatini identity (40.43).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Example 40.10 cites the equation numbers of Rules 1 and 2 the wrong way round.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Underlined M denotes the matrix of metric components, with M_{mu nu} = g_{mu nu} and (M^-1) entries g^{mu nu}.

rho_0 rest-mass density, u specific internal energy, rho = rho_0(1+u) total energy density, p pressure, w flow-line tangent d/dtau, v normalized 4-velocity, vdot^alpha = v^alpha_{;beta} v^beta acceleration, K displacement field, J = rho_0 v current.
L = -(1/4) F F with no 4 pi, i.e. Heaviside-Lorentz-type units.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Gaussian-unit texts carry an extra 1/(4 pi) (or 1/(16 pi)).

notation_and_conventions.convention: T denotes the string's kinetic energy in Example 40.2, a calligraphic T is the string tension, and bold T (components T^{mu nu}) is the energy-momentum tensor.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Keep the three apart when moving from the string example to the Hilbert tensor; the tension carries a script font in eqns 40.7 and 40.21.

notable.summary: For a unit-mass particle with Lagrangian one half of the metric contracted with two velocity factors, obtain the geodesic equation, build the Hamiltonian, re-derive geodesics from Hamilton's equations, and ask what follows when a metric component does not depend on some coordinate.

notable.summary: Specialize the particle Lagrangian to Schwarzschild spacetime, compute the conjugate momenta, show the Hamiltonian equals the Lagrangian, and use Hamilton's equations to show p_t and p_phi are conserved.

notable.summary: For the flat-space scalar Lagrangian, find the momentum density, the Hamiltonian density (which matches T_00) and the momentum-like quantities dL/d(d_mu phi).
notable.why_notable: Shows the Hamiltonian density equals the energy density of eqn 40.63, tying the Hamiltonian and energy-momentum pictures together.

notable.summary: Define the continuous angular-momentum tensor from T and a rank-3 flux M built from positions and T; show its conservation in flat spacetime requires T to be symmetric.

notable.summary: Check that the collected fluid-variation terms in eqn 40.88 are compatible with local mass conservation as expanded in eqn 40.86.

difficulty.notes: The flat-space part (40.1-40.3) is gentle and well paced. The Einstein-Hilbert variation needs fluent index work, three variation identities (one quoted without proof) and several printed label and sign slips must be corrected mentally. Noether's theorem is compressed, skipping the steps that make the Lie-derivative argument work. The fluid section is long, heuristic in its middle step, and explicitly optional. Physical motivation for choosing R as the gravitational Lagrangian is thin.
